title: OTA wants public input on east-west connector interchange - NewsBreak
text:
By Tanner DeLeon/ ,
1 hours ago
OKLAHOMA CITY ( KFOR ) — The Oklahoma Turnpike Authority is moving into the next phase of its controversial Turnpike expansion plans, but they want to make sure they don’t run into any unexpected hiccups.
They are now asking for the public’s help as they look to begin construction next year.
The east-west connection would go from I-44 near Newcastle, between Moore and Norman, then connect the Kickapoo Turnpike out by Newalla.
It is being built in three phases.
The OTA says it needs public input to complete the design for phase two, so everything goes smoothly.
OTA makes controversial vote as fight over ACCESS OK continues “We’re just really looking for some comments about what traffic is like now and what they’re hoping to see as far as improvements for this interchange,” Lisa Shearer-Salim with the OTA said.
Before crews are set to break ground, the OTA is looking for public input on a new interchange at I-44 in McClain County.
“Those people who are driving that section of I-40 for every single day who are very familiar with it, what improvements do they want to see?” Shearer-Salim asked. “What do they think about these improvements that we’re proposing, and how could that impact them? Is there anything in that area that we may not know about that they see on a daily basis that they could share with us that might help us improve the design process?”
The OTA says knowing where drivers want on-and-off ramps, and pinpointing the worst traffic spots, can help them as they build and finalize the route, which in turn lets those who live on the path know whether or not their property will be affected.
“We’re very close to the completion of the design phase of this interchange, and this is one of the final steps to be able to complete that design work,” Shearer-Salim said.
With phase one set to begin early next year, the OTA says it is trying to avoid anything that would potentially delay the start of phase two.
“There’s always that potential because we do take the public input into consideration, but we don’t expect that to delay any part of the process,” Shearer-Salim said.
For anyone looking to provide any type of input, you can do so online .
You have until December 3rd to provide a comment.
